nodes.name: Polynomial optimization problem P
nodes.statement: Recent years have seen the development of (global) semi-algebraic optimization and in particular LP- or semidefinite relaxations for the polynomial optimization problem: \begin{equation} \mathbf{P}:\quad f^*=\displaystyle\min_\mathbf{x}\:\{f(\mathbf{x})\::\: \mathbf{x}\in\mathbf{K}\:\} \end{equation} where $f\in\mathbb{R}[\mathbf{x}]$ is a polynomial and $\mathbf{K}\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ is the basic semi-algebraic set \begin{equation} \mathbf{K}\,=\,\{\,\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n\::\: g_j(\mathbf{x})\,\geq\,0,\quad j=1,\ldots,m\}, \end{equation} for some polynomials $g_j\in\mathbb{R}[\mathbf{x}]$, $j=1,\ldots,m$.
nodes.statement_short: Minimize a polynomial $f$ over a basic semi-algebraic set $\mathbf{K}=\{g_j\geq0\}$; optimal value $f^*$.

nodes.name: Problem P: f* = min f over K
nodes.statement: \mathbf{P}:\quad f^*=\displaystyle\min_\mathbf{x}\:\{f(\mathbf{x})\::\: \mathbf{x}\in\mathbf{K}\:\}
nodes.label: def-pb

nodes.name: Basic semi-algebraic set K
nodes.statement: \mathbf{K}\,=\,\{\,\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n\::\: g_j(\mathbf{x})\,\geq\,0,\quad j=1,\ldots,m\},
nodes.label: setk

nodes.name: Semidefinite relaxations (Putinar-based hierarchy)
nodes.statement: {\it Semidefinite} relaxations based on Putinar's certificate of positivity on $\mathbf{K}$ \cite{Putinar93}, where the $d$-th convex relaxation of the hierarchy is a semidefinite program which solves the optimization problem \begin{equation} \gamma_d=\max_{t,\sigma_j}\:\{\,t\::\: f-t=\sigma_0+\sum_{j=1}^n \sigma_j\,g_j\}. \end{equation} The unknowns $\sigma_j$ are sums of squares polynomials with the degree bound constraint ${\rm degree}\,\sigma_jg_j\leq 2d$, $j=0,\ldots,m$, and the expression in (\ref{put-cert}) is a certificate of positivity on $\mathbf{K}$ for the polynomial $\mathbf{x}\mapsto f(\mathbf{x})-t$.
nodes.statement_short: The $d$-th SDP relaxation maximizes $t$ such that $f-t=\sigma_0+\sum_j\sigma_j g_j$ with SOS $\sigma_j$ of bounded degree.

nodes.name: SDP relaxation value gamma_d
nodes.statement: \gamma_d=\max_{t,\sigma_j}\:\{\,t\::\: f-t=\sigma_0+\sum_{j=1}^n \sigma_j\,g_j\}.
nodes.label: put-cert

nodes.name: LP-relaxations (Krivine-Stengle-based hierarchy)
nodes.statement: {\it LP}-relaxations based on Krivine-Stengle's certificate of positivity on $\mathbf{K}$ \cite{Krivine64a,Stengle74}, where the $d$-th convex relaxation of the hierarchy is a linear program which solves the optimization problem \begin{eqnarray} \nonumber \theta_d\,=\,\max_{\lambda\geq0,t}\:\left\{t\::\: f-t\right.&=&\sum_{(\alpha,\beta)\in\mathbb{N}^{2m}_{d}}\lambda_{\alpha\beta}\,\left(\prod_{j=1}^mg_j^{\alpha_j}\right)\times\\ &&\left.\left(\prod_{j=1}^m(1-g_j)^{\beta_j}\right)\right\}, \end{eqnarray} where $\mathbb{N}^{2m}_{d}=\{(\alpha,\beta)\in\mathbb{N}^{2m}:\sum_j\alpha_j+\beta_j\leq d\}$. The unknown are $t$ and the nonnegative scalars $\lambda=(\lambda_{\alpha\beta})$, and it is assumed that $0\leq g_j\leq 1$ on $\mathbf{K}$ (possibly after scaling) and the family $\{g_i,1-g_i\}$ generates the algebra $\mathbb{R}[\mathbf{x}]$ of polynomials.
nodes.statement_short: The $d$-th LP relaxation maximizes $t$ such that $f-t$ is a nonnegative combination of products $\prod g_j^{\alpha_j}(1-g_j)^{\beta_j}$ of degree $\leq d$.

nodes.name: LP relaxation value theta_d
nodes.statement: \nonumber \theta_d\,=\,\max_{\lambda\geq0,t}\:\left\{t\::\: f-t\right.&=&\sum_{(\alpha,\beta)\in\mathbb{N}^{2m}_{d}}\lambda_{\alpha\beta}\,\left(\prod_{j=1}^mg_j^{\alpha_j}\right)\times\\ &&\left.\left(\prod_{j=1}^m(1-g_j)^{\beta_j}\right)\right\},
nodes.label: kriv-cert

nodes.name: Convergence of SDP and LP hierarchies
nodes.statement: In both cases, $(\gamma_d)$ and $(\theta_d)$, $d\in\mathbb{N}$, provide two monotone nondecreasing sequences of lower bounds on $f^*$ and if $\mathbf{K}$ is compact then both converge to $f^*$ as one let $d$ increase.
conclusions: $(\gamma_d)$ and $(\theta_d)$, $d\in\mathbb{N}$, provide two monotone nondecreasing sequences of lower bounds on $f^*$
both converge to $f^*$ as one let $d$ increase

nodes.name: LP-relaxations cannot be exact for convex problems
nodes.statement: For instance, it has been shown in \cite{Lasserre02a,lasserre-imperial} that the LP-relaxations {\it cannot} be exact for most convex problems, i.e., the sequence of the associated optimal values converges to the global optimum only {\it asymptotically} and not in finitely many steps.
conclusions: the LP-relaxations {\it cannot} be exact

nodes.name: Finite convergence of SDP relaxations for convex problems
nodes.statement: This is in contrast with the semidefinite relaxations (\ref{put-cert}) for which finite convergence takes place for convex problems where $\nabla^2f(\mathbf{x}^*)$ is positive definite at every minimizer $\mathbf{x}^*\in\mathbf{K}$ (see de Klerk and Laurent \cite[Corollary 3.3]{deklerk-convex}) and occurs at the first relaxation for SOS-convex\footnote{An SOS-convex polynomial is a convex polynomial whose Hessian factors as $L(\mathbf{x})L(\mathbf{x})^T$ for some rectangular matrix polynomial $L$. For instance, separable convex polynomials are SOS-convex.} problems \cite[Theorem 3.3]{lasserre-convex}.
assumptions: convex problems where $\nabla^2f(\mathbf{x}^*)$ is positive definite at every minimizer $\mathbf{x}^*\in\mathbf{K}$
conclusions: finite convergence takes place
nodes.statement_short: SDP relaxations converge finitely for convex problems with positive definite Hessian at minimizers, and at the first step for SOS-convex problems.

nodes.name: SOS-convex polynomial
nodes.statement: An SOS-convex polynomial is a convex polynomial whose Hessian factors as $L(\mathbf{x})L(\mathbf{x})^T$ for some rectangular matrix polynomial $L$.
differentia: whose Hessian factors as $L(\mathbf{x})L(\mathbf{x})^T$ for some rectangular matrix polynomial $L$

nodes.name: Genericity of finite convergence (Nie)
nodes.statement: In fact, as demonstrated in recent works of Marshall \cite{Marshall2} and Nie \cite{nie2012}, finite convergence is generic (even for non convex problems).
conclusions: finite convergence is generic (even for non convex problems)

nodes.name: Dual function G_d of the Lagrangian hierarchy
nodes.statement: Each relaxation in the hierarchy is a finite-dimensional convex optimization problem of the form: \begin{equation} \rho_d\,=\,\max_{{\boldmath{\lambda}}}\:\{\:G_d(\lambda)\::\: {\boldmath{\lambda}}\geq0\}, \end{equation} where $G_d(\cdot)$ is the concave function defined by: \begin{eqnarray} \nonumber G_d(\lambda)\,:=\,\min_\mathbf{x}\:\left\{f(\mathbf{x})\right.&-&\sum_{(\alpha,\beta)\in\mathbb{N}^{2m}_{d}}\lambda_{\alpha\beta}\,\left(\prod_{j=1}^mg_j^{\alpha_j}(\mathbf{x})\right)\times\\ &&\left. \left(\prod_{j=1}^m(1-g_j(\mathbf{x}))^{\beta_j}\right)\:\right\}.\end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: $\rho_d$ maximizes over $\lambda\geq0$ the concave dual function $G_d(\lambda)$, the unconstrained minimum of $f$ minus a $\lambda$-weighted sum of products of $g_j$ and $1-g_j$.

nodes.name: Definition of G_d(lambda)
nodes.statement: \nonumber G_d(\lambda)\,:=\,\min_\mathbf{x}\:\left\{f(\mathbf{x})\right.&-&\sum_{(\alpha,\beta)\in\mathbb{N}^{2m}_{d}}\lambda_{\alpha\beta}\,\left(\prod_{j=1}^mg_j^{\alpha_j}(\mathbf{x})\right)\times\\ &&\left. \left(\prod_{j=1}^m(1-g_j(\mathbf{x}))^{\beta_j}\right)\:\right\}.
nodes.label: def-gedelambda

nodes.name: rho_d dominates the LP bound theta_d
nodes.statement: (a) $\rho_d\geq\theta_d$ for all $d$, and so $\rho_d\to f^*$ as one let $d$ increase.
conclusions: $\rho_d\geq\theta_d$ for all $d$
$\rho_d\to f^*$ as one let $d$ increase

nodes.name: rho_d beats Sherali-Adams RLT for 0/1 programs
nodes.statement: (c) For $0/1$ optimization, i.e., when $\mathbf{K}\subseteq\{0,1\}^n$, finite convergence takes place and the optimal value $\rho_d$ provides a better lower bound than the one obtained with Sherali-Adams' RLT hierarchy \cite{SheraliAdams90}.
conclusions: finite convergence takes place
the optimal value $\rho_d$ provides a better lower bound than the one obtained with Sherali-Adams' RLT hierarchy

nodes.name: Justification of the comparison with Sherali-Adams
nodes.statement: In fact, the latter is solving (\ref{kriv-cert}) with only a subset of the products that appear in (\ref{kriv-cert}).
nodes.statement_short: Direct: Sherali-Adams uses only a subset of the products in the LP hierarchy, so the Lagrangian hierarchy dominates it.

nodes.name: Problem P-tilde_d with redundant product constraints
nodes.statement: To see this, consider the optimization problem $\tilde{\mathbf{P}}_d$ defined by: \begin{equation} \min_\mathbf{x}\:\{f(\mathbf{x})\::\:g_j(\mathbf{x})^{\alpha_j}(1-g_j(\mathbf{x}))^{\beta_j}\,\geq\,0,\: (\alpha,\beta)\in\mathbb{N}^{2m}_{d}\}\end{equation} which has same value $f^*$ as $\mathbf{P}$ because $\tilde{\mathbf{P}}_d$ is just $\mathbf{P}$ with additional redundant constraints; and notice that $\tilde{\mathbf{P}}_1=\mathbf{P}$.
nodes.statement_short: $\tilde{\mathbf{P}}_d$ is $\mathbf{P}$ with the redundant product constraints $g_j^{\alpha_j}(1-g_j)^{\beta_j}\geq0$, $|\alpha+\beta|\leq d$, added; same optimal value.

nodes.name: Problem P-tilde_d
nodes.statement: \min_\mathbf{x}\:\{f(\mathbf{x})\::\:g_j(\mathbf{x})^{\alpha_j}(1-g_j(\mathbf{x}))^{\beta_j}\,\geq\,0,\: (\alpha,\beta)\in\mathbb{N}^{2m}_{d}\}
nodes.label: pbtildeP

nodes.name: Lagrangian L_d(x, lambda)
nodes.statement: Even though (\ref{newhierarchy-def}) is a convex optimization problem, evaluating $G_d(\lambda)$ at a point $\lambda\geq0$ requires computing the unconstrained global minimum of the function \begin{eqnarray} \nonumber \mathbf{x}\mapsto L_d(\mathbf{x},\lambda)&:=& f(\mathbf{x})-\sum_{(\alpha,\beta)\in\mathbb{N}^{2m}_{d}}\lambda_{\alpha\beta}\,\left(\prod_{j=1}^mg_j(\mathbf{x})^{\alpha_j}\right) \times\\ &&\left(\prod_{j=1}^m(1-g_j(\mathbf{x}))^{\beta_j}\right),\end{eqnarray} an NP-hard problem in general.
nodes.statement_short: Evaluating $G_d(\lambda)$ requires globally minimizing the Lagrangian $L_d(\cdot,\lambda)$, NP-hard in general.

nodes.name: Lagrangian L_d
nodes.statement: \nonumber \mathbf{x}\mapsto L_d(\mathbf{x},\lambda)&:=& f(\mathbf{x})-\sum_{(\alpha,\beta)\in\mathbb{N}^{2m}_{d}}\lambda_{\alpha\beta}\,\left(\prod_{j=1}^mg_j(\mathbf{x})^{\alpha_j}\right) \times\\ &&\left(\prod_{j=1}^m(1-g_j(\mathbf{x}))^{\beta_j}\right),
nodes.label: functionL

nodes.name: Polynomial ring R[x]
nodes.statement: Let $\mathbb{R}[\mathbf{x}]$ be the ring of polynomials in the variables $\mathbf{x}=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$.

nodes.name: Polynomials of degree at most d
nodes.statement: Denote by $\mathbb{R}[\mathbf{x}]_d\subset\mathbb{R}[\mathbf{x}]$ the vector space of polynomials of degree at most $d$, which forms a vector space of dimension $s(d)={n+d\choose d}$, with e.g., the usual canonical basis $(\mathbf{x}^\alpha)$ of monomials.

nodes.name: Sums of squares polynomials
nodes.statement: Also, denote by $\Sigma[\mathbf{x}]\subset\mathbb{R}[\mathbf{x}]$ (resp. $\Sigma[\mathbf{x}]_d\subset\mathbb{R}[\mathbf{x}]_{2d}$) the space of sums of squares (s.o.s.) polynomials (resp. s.o.s. polynomials of degree at most $2d$).
nodes.genus: space of sums of squares (s.o.s.) polynomials

nodes.name: Symmetric matrices and positive semidefiniteness
nodes.statement: Finally, let $\mathcal{S}^n$ denote the space of $n\times n$ real symmetric matrices, with inner product $\langle \mathbf{A},\mathbf{B}\rangle ={\rm trace}\,\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}$, and where the notation $\mathbf{A}\succeq0$ (resp. $\mathbf{A}\succ0$) stands for $\mathbf{A}$ is positive semidefinite.
nodes.genus: space of $n\times n$ real symmetric matrices

nodes.name: Quadratic module
nodes.statement: With $g_0:=1$, the quadratic module $Q(g_1,\ldots,g_m)\subset\mathbb{R}[\mathbf{x}]$ generated by polynomials $g_1,\ldots,g_m$, is defined by \[Q(g_1,\ldots,g_m)\,:=\,\{\sum_{j=0}^m\sigma_j\,g_j\::\:\sigma_j\in\Sigma[\mathbf{x}]\}.\]
nodes.statement_short: The quadratic module generated by $g_1,\dots,g_m$ is the set of SOS-weighted combinations $\sum_j\sigma_j g_j$ with $g_0=1$.

nodes.name: Putinar's and Krivine-Stengle's Positivstellensätze
nodes.statement: Let $g_0=1$ and $\mathbf{K}$ in (\ref{setk}) be compact. (a) If the quadratic polynomial $\mathbf{x}\mapsto M-\Vert\mathbf{x}\Vert^2$ belongs to $Q(g_1,\ldots,g_m)$ and if $f\in\mathbb{R}[\mathbf{x}]$ is strictly positive on $\mathbf{K}$ then $f\in Q(g_1,\ldots,g_m)$. (b) Assume that $0\leq g_j\leq 1$ on $\mathbf{K}$ for every $j$, and the family $\{g_j,1-g_j\}$ generates $\mathbb{R}[\mathbf{x}]$. If $f$ is strictly positive on $\mathbf{K}$ then \[f\,=\,\sum_{\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{N}^m}c_{\alpha\beta}\,\prod_{j}g_j^{\alpha_j}\,\prod_{\ell}(1-g_\ell)^{\beta_\ell},\] for some finitely many nonnegative scalars $(c_{\alpha\beta})$.
assumptions: the quadratic polynomial $\mathbf{x}\mapsto M-\Vert\mathbf{x}\Vert^2$ belongs to $Q(g_1,\ldots,g_m)$
$0\leq g_j\leq 1$ on $\mathbf{K}$ for every $j$, and the family $\{g_j,1-g_j\}$ generates $\mathbb{R}[\mathbf{x}]$
conclusions: $f\in Q(g_1,\ldots,g_m)$
\[f\,=\,\sum_{\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{N}^m}c_{\alpha\beta}\,\prod_{j}g_j^{\alpha_j}\,\prod_{\ell}(1-g_\ell)^{\beta_\ell},\] for some finitely many nonnegative scalars $(c_{\alpha\beta})$
nodes.statement_short: On compact $\mathbf{K}$, positive polynomials lie in the Archimedean quadratic module (Putinar) or are nonnegative combinations of products of $g_j$, $1-g_j$ (Krivine-Stengle).

nodes.name: Compactness and generating family assumption
nodes.statement: $\mathbf{K}$ is compact and $0\leq g_j\leq 1$ on $\mathbf{K}$ for all $j=1,\ldots,m$. Moreover, the family of polynomials $\{g_j, 1-g_j\}$ generates the algebra $\mathbb{R}[\mathbf{x}]$.
nodes.label: ass1

nodes.name: Assumption 1 can always be enforced
nodes.statement: Notice that if $\mathbf{K}$ is compact and Assumption \ref{ass1} does not hold, one may always rescale the variables $x_i$ so as to have $\mathbf{K}\subset [0,1]^n$, and then add redundant constraints $0\leq x_i\leq 1$ for all $i=1,\ldots,m$. Then the family $\{g_j,1-g_j\}$ (which includes $x_j$ and $1-x_j$ for all $j$) generates the algebra $\mathbb{R}[\mathbf{x}]$ and Assumption \ref{ass1} holds.
nodes.statement_short: For compact $\mathbf{K}$, rescaling into $[0,1]^n$ and adding bounds $0\leq x_i\leq1$ makes Assumption 1 hold.

nodes.name: Lagrangian relaxation hierarchy rho_d
nodes.statement: With $d\in\mathbb{N}$ and $0\leq \lambda=(\lambda_{\alpha\beta})$, $(\alpha,\beta)\in\mathbb{N}^{2m}_{d}$, let $\lambda\mapsto G_d(\lambda)$ be the function defined in (\ref{def-gedelambda}), with associated problem: \begin{equation} \rho_d\,=\,\max_{{\boldmath{\lambda}}}\:\{\:G_d(\lambda)\::\: {\boldmath{\lambda}}\geq0\}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: $\rho_d=\max_{\lambda\geq0}G_d(\lambda)$: maximize the dual function of the redundant-constraint Lagrangian.

nodes.name: Lagrangian hierarchy rho_d (formal)
nodes.statement: \rho_d\,=\,\max_{{\boldmath{\lambda}}}\:\{\:G_d(\lambda)\::\: {\boldmath{\lambda}}\geq0\}.
nodes.label: newhierarchy-def1

nodes.name: Weak duality and Lagrangian interpretation of rho_d
nodes.statement: Observe that $G_d(\lambda)\leq f^*$ for all $\lambda\geq0$, and computing $\rho_d$ is just solving the Lagrangian relaxation of problem $\tilde{\mathbf{P}}_d$ in (\ref{pbtildeP}).
conclusions: $G_d(\lambda)\leq f^*$
computing $\rho_d$ is just solving the Lagrangian relaxation of problem $\tilde{\mathbf{P}}_d$ in (\ref{pbtildeP})

nodes.name: Convergence of the Lagrangian hierarchy
nodes.statement: Let $\mathbf{K}$ be as in (\ref{setk}), $f\in\mathbb{R}[\mathbf{x}]$, $d\in\mathbb{N}$, and let Assumption \ref{ass1} hold. Consider problem (\ref{newhierarchy-def1}) associated with $\mathbf{P}$ and with optimal value $\rho_d$. Then the sequence $(\rho_d)$, $d\in\mathbb{N}$, is monotone nondecreasing and $\rho_d\to f^*$ as $d\to\infty$.
assumptions: $\mathbf{K}$ be as in (\ref{setk}), $f\in\mathbb{R}[\mathbf{x}]$, $d\in\mathbb{N}$, and let Assumption \ref{ass1} hold
conclusions: the sequence $(\rho_d)$, $d\in\mathbb{N}$, is monotone nondecreasing and $\rho_d\to f^*$ as $d\to\infty$
nodes.statement_short: Under Assumption 1, the Lagrangian hierarchy values $\rho_d$ increase monotonically to $f^*$.
nodes.label: thmain

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2.2
nodes.statement: We first prove that $\rho_{d+1}\geq\rho_d$ for all $d$, so that the sequence $(\rho_d)$, $d\in\mathbb{N}$, is monotone nondecreasing. Let $0\leq\lambda=(\lambda_{\alpha\beta})$ with $(\alpha,\beta)\in\mathbb{N}^{2m}_{d}$. Then $0\leq\tilde{\lambda}$ with $\tilde{\lambda}_{\alpha\beta}=\lambda_{\alpha\beta}$ whenever $(\alpha,\beta)\in\mathbb{N}^{2m}_{d}$, and $\tilde{\lambda}_{\alpha\beta}=0$ whenever $\vert\alpha+\beta\vert>d$, is such that $G_{d+1}(\tilde{\lambda})=G_{d}(\lambda)$ and so $\rho_{d+1}\geq\rho_d$. Next, let $\epsilon>0$ be fixed, arbitrary. The polynomial $f-f^*+\epsilon$ is positive on $\mathbf{K}$ and therefore, by \cite{Stengle74}, \cite[Theorem 2.23]{lasserre-imperial}, \[f-(f^*-\epsilon)\,=\,\sum_{(\alpha,\beta)\in\mathbb{N}^{2m}_d}c^\epsilon_{\alpha\beta}\,\left(\prod_{j=1}^mg_j^{\alpha_j}\right)\left(\prod_{j=1}^m(1-g_j)^{\beta_j}\right),\] for some nonnegative vector of coefficients $\mathbf{c}^\epsilon=(c_{\alpha\beta}^\epsilon)$. Equivalently, \[f-\sum_{(\alpha,\beta)\in\mathbb{N}^{2m}_d}c^\epsilon_{\alpha\beta}\,\left(\prod_{j=1}^mg_j^{\alpha_j}\right)\left(\prod_{j=1}^m(1-g_j)^{\beta_j}\right)\,=\,(f^*-\epsilon).\] Letting \[d_\epsilon\,:=\,\max_{\alpha,\beta}\:\{\vert\alpha+\beta\vert\::\:c^\epsilon_{\alpha\beta}>0\},\] we obtain $f^*\geq G_{d_\epsilon}(\mathbf{c}^\epsilon)\,=\,f^*-\epsilon$. And so \[f^*\,\geq\,\max_\lambda\{G_{d_\epsilon}(\lambda)\,:\,\lambda\geq0\}\,\geq\,f^*-\epsilon.\] As $\epsilon>0$ was arbitrary, the desired result follows.
nodes.statement_short: Monotonicity by zero-padding multipliers; convergence by applying the Krivine-Stengle certificate to $f-f^*+\epsilon$ and using its coefficients as multipliers.

nodes.name: Goal: monotonicity
nodes.statement: We first prove that $\rho_{d+1}\geq\rho_d$ for all $d$, so that the sequence $(\rho_d)$, $d\in\mathbb{N}$, is monotone nondecreasing.
nodes.statement_short: State the first goal: monotonicity of $\rho_d$.

nodes.name: Pad multipliers with zeros
nodes.statement: Let $0\leq\lambda=(\lambda_{\alpha\beta})$ with $(\alpha,\beta)\in\mathbb{N}^{2m}_{d}$. Then $0\leq\tilde{\lambda}$ with $\tilde{\lambda}_{\alpha\beta}=\lambda_{\alpha\beta}$ whenever $(\alpha,\beta)\in\mathbb{N}^{2m}_{d}$, and $\tilde{\lambda}_{\alpha\beta}=0$ whenever $\vert\alpha+\beta\vert>d$, is such that $G_{d+1}(\tilde{\lambda})=G_{d}(\lambda)$ and so $\rho_{d+1}\geq\rho_d$.
nodes.statement_short: Extend $\lambda$ by zeros to get $G_{d+1}(\tilde\lambda)=G_d(\lambda)$, hence monotonicity.

nodes.name: Apply Krivine-Stengle certificate
nodes.statement: Next, let $\epsilon>0$ be fixed, arbitrary. The polynomial $f-f^*+\epsilon$ is positive on $\mathbf{K}$ and therefore, by \cite{Stengle74}, \cite[Theorem 2.23]{lasserre-imperial}, \[f-(f^*-\epsilon)\,=\,\sum_{(\alpha,\beta)\in\mathbb{N}^{2m}_d}c^\epsilon_{\alpha\beta}\,\left(\prod_{j=1}^mg_j^{\alpha_j}\right)\left(\prod_{j=1}^m(1-g_j)^{\beta_j}\right),\] for some nonnegative vector of coefficients $\mathbf{c}^\epsilon=(c_{\alpha\beta}^\epsilon)$. Equivalently, \[f-\sum_{(\alpha,\beta)\in\mathbb{N}^{2m}_d}c^\epsilon_{\alpha\beta}\,\left(\prod_{j=1}^mg_j^{\alpha_j}\right)\left(\prod_{j=1}^m(1-g_j)^{\beta_j}\right)\,=\,(f^*-\epsilon).\]
nodes.statement_short: Represent $f-f^*+\epsilon$ via the Krivine-Stengle Positivstellensatz with nonnegative coefficients.

nodes.name: Bound rho at level d_epsilon
nodes.statement: Letting \[d_\epsilon\,:=\,\max_{\alpha,\beta}\:\{\vert\alpha+\beta\vert\::\:c^\epsilon_{\alpha\beta}>0\},\] we obtain $f^*\geq G_{d_\epsilon}(\mathbf{c}^\epsilon)\,=\,f^*-\epsilon$. And so \[f^*\,\geq\,\max_\lambda\{G_{d_\epsilon}(\lambda)\,:\,\lambda\geq0\}\,\geq\,f^*-\epsilon.\]
nodes.statement_short: Use the certificate coefficients as multipliers: $\rho_{d_\epsilon}\geq f^*-\epsilon$.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: As $\epsilon>0$ was arbitrary, the desired result follows.
nodes.statement_short: Let $\epsilon\to0$.

nodes.name: Lagrangian relaxation with redundant constraints is asymptotically exact
nodes.statement: Let $\mathbf{K}$ be as in (\ref{setk}), Assumption (\ref{ass1}) hold and let $\tilde{\mathbf{P}}_d$, $d\in\mathbb{N}$, be as in (\ref{pbtildeP}). Then for every $\epsilon>0$ there exists $d_\epsilon\in\mathbb{N}$ such that for every $d\geq d_\epsilon$, the Lagrangian relaxation of $\tilde{\mathbf{P}}_d$, yields a lower bound $f^*-\epsilon\leq \rho_d\leq f^*$.
assumptions: $\mathbf{K}$ be as in (\ref{setk}), Assumption (\ref{ass1}) hold and let $\tilde{\mathbf{P}}_d$, $d\in\mathbb{N}$, be as in (\ref{pbtildeP})
conclusions: for every $\epsilon>0$ there exists $d_\epsilon\in\mathbb{N}$ such that for every $d\geq d_\epsilon$, the Lagrangian relaxation of $\tilde{\mathbf{P}}_d$, yields a lower bound $f^*-\epsilon\leq \rho_d\leq f^*$
nodes.statement_short: Lagrangian relaxation of $\mathbf{P}$ with enough redundant product constraints gives lower bounds arbitrarily close to $f^*$.
nodes.label: lagrangian

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 2.1
nodes.statement: This follows from Theorem \ref{thmain} and the fact that computing $\rho_d$ is just solving the Lagrangian relaxation associated with $\tilde{\mathbf{P}}_d$.
nodes.statement_short: Immediate from Theorem 2.2 since $\rho_d$ is the Lagrangian relaxation value of $\tilde{\mathbf{P}}_d$.

nodes.name: Rationale for adding redundant constraints
nodes.statement: So the interpretation of Corollary \ref{lagrangian} is that the Lagrangian relaxation technique in non convex optimization can provide a lower bound as close as desired to the global optimum $f^*$ provided that it is applied to an equivalent formulation of $\mathbf{P}$ that contains sufficiently many redundant constraints which are products of the original ones. It also provides a rigorous rationale for the well-known fact that adding redundant constraints helps solve $\mathbf{P}$. Indeed, even though the new problems $\tilde{\mathbf{P}}_d$, $d\in\mathbb{N}$, are all equivalent to $\mathbf{P}$, their Lagrangian relaxations are not equivalent to that of $\mathbf{P}$.
nodes.statement_short: Adding redundant product constraints does not change $\mathbf{P}$ but strengthens its Lagrangian relaxation, explaining why redundant constraints help.

nodes.name: First-step exactness of the Lagrangian hierarchy for convex programs
nodes.statement: Let $\mathbf{K}$ be as in (\ref{setk}) and assume that $f$ and $-g_j$ are convex, $j=1,\ldots,m$. Moreover, assume that Slater's condition\footnote{Slater's condition holds for $\mathbf{P}$ if there exists $\mathbf{x}_0\in\mathbf{K}$ such that $g_j(\mathbf{x}_0)>0$ for every $j=1,\ldots,m$.} holds and $f^*>-\infty$. Then the hierarchy of convex relaxations (\ref{newhierarchy-def}) has finite convergence at step $d=1$, i.e., $\rho_1=f^*$, and $\rho_1=G_1(\lambda^*)$ for some nonnegative $\lambda^*\in\mathbb{R}^m$.
conclusions: the hierarchy of convex relaxations (\ref{newhierarchy-def}) has finite convergence at step $d=1$, i.e., $\rho_1=f^*$, and $\rho_1=G_1(\lambda^*)$ for some nonnegative $\lambda^*\in\mathbb{R}^m$
nodes.statement_short: For convex $\mathbf{P}$ with Slater's condition, $\rho_1=f^*$ and the dual optimum is attained.
nodes.label: new-convex-case

nodes.name: Slater's condition
nodes.statement: Slater's condition holds for $\mathbf{P}$ if there exists $\mathbf{x}_0\in\mathbf{K}$ such that $g_j(\mathbf{x}_0)>0$ for every $j=1,\ldots,m$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2.3
nodes.statement: This is because the dual method applied to $\mathbf{P}$ (i.e. $\tilde{\mathbf{P}}_1$) converges, i.e., \begin{eqnarray*} f^*&=&\max_{\lambda\geq0}\:\left\{\min_\mathbf{x}\:\{f(\mathbf{x})-\sum_{j=1}^m\lambda_j\,g_j(\mathbf{x})\}\right\}\\ &=&\max_\lambda\{G_1(\lambda)\,:\,\lambda\geq0\}\,=\,\rho_1.\end{eqnarray*} Next, let $\lambda^{(n)}$ be a maximizing sequence, i.e., $G_1(\lambda^{(n)})\to f^*$ as $n\to\infty$. Since Slater's condition holds (say at some $\mathbf{x}_0\in\mathbf{K}$), one has \[G_1(\lambda^{(0)})\,\leq\,G_1(\lambda^{(n)})\,\leq\,f(\mathbf{x}_0)-\sum_{j=1}^m\lambda^{(n)}_j\,g_j(\mathbf{x}_0),\] for all $n$, and so $\lambda^{(n)}_j\leq (f(\mathbf{x}_0)-G_1(\lambda^{(0)}))/g_j(\mathbf{x}_0)$ for every $j=1,\ldots,m$, and all $n\geq1$. So there is a subsequence $(n_k)$, $k\in\mathbb{N}$, and $\lambda^*\in\mathbb{R}^m_+$, such that $\lambda^{(n_k)}\to\lambda^*\geq0$ as $k\to\infty$. Finally, let $\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n$ be fixed, arbitrary. From \[G_1(\lambda^{(n_k)})\,\leq\,f(\mathbf{x})-\sum_{j=1}^m\lambda^{(n_k)}_j\,g_j(\mathbf{x}),\qquad\forall\,k,\] letting $k\to\infty$ yields \[f^*\,\leq\,f(\mathbf{x})-\sum_{j=1}^m\lambda^*_j\,g_j(\mathbf{x}).\] As $\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n$ was arbitrary, this proves $G_1(\lambda^*)\geq f^*$, which combined with $G_1(\lambda^*)\leq f^*$ yields the desired result $G_1(\lambda^*)=f^*$.
nodes.statement_short: Strong Lagrangian duality gives $\rho_1=f^*$; Slater's point bounds a maximizing sequence, whose limit point attains $G_1(\lambda^*)=f^*$.

nodes.name: Strong duality
nodes.statement: This is because the dual method applied to $\mathbf{P}$ (i.e. $\tilde{\mathbf{P}}_1$) converges, i.e., \begin{eqnarray*} f^*&=&\max_{\lambda\geq0}\:\left\{\min_\mathbf{x}\:\{f(\mathbf{x})-\sum_{j=1}^m\lambda_j\,g_j(\mathbf{x})\}\right\}\\ &=&\max_\lambda\{G_1(\lambda)\,:\,\lambda\geq0\}\,=\,\rho_1.\end{eqnarray*}
nodes.statement_short: Convex duality: the dual method converges, so $\rho_1=f^*$.

nodes.name: Bounded maximizing sequence
nodes.statement: Next, let $\lambda^{(n)}$ be a maximizing sequence, i.e., $G_1(\lambda^{(n)})\to f^*$ as $n\to\infty$. Since Slater's condition holds (say at some $\mathbf{x}_0\in\mathbf{K}$), one has \[G_1(\lambda^{(0)})\,\leq\,G_1(\lambda^{(n)})\,\leq\,f(\mathbf{x}_0)-\sum_{j=1}^m\lambda^{(n)}_j\,g_j(\mathbf{x}_0),\] for all $n$, and so $\lambda^{(n)}_j\leq (f(\mathbf{x}_0)-G_1(\lambda^{(0)}))/g_j(\mathbf{x}_0)$ for every $j=1,\ldots,m$, and all $n\geq1$. So there is a subsequence $(n_k)$, $k\in\mathbb{N}$, and $\lambda^*\in\mathbb{R}^m_+$, such that $\lambda^{(n_k)}\to\lambda^*\geq0$ as $k\to\infty$.
nodes.statement_short: Slater's point bounds the multipliers; extract a convergent subsequence.

nodes.name: Pass to the limit
nodes.statement: Finally, let $\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n$ be fixed, arbitrary. From \[G_1(\lambda^{(n_k)})\,\leq\,f(\mathbf{x})-\sum_{j=1}^m\lambda^{(n_k)}_j\,g_j(\mathbf{x}),\qquad\forall\,k,\] letting $k\to\infty$ yields \[f^*\,\leq\,f(\mathbf{x})-\sum_{j=1}^m\lambda^*_j\,g_j(\mathbf{x}).\]
nodes.statement_short: Take limits in the dual inequality at a fixed $\mathbf{x}$.

nodes.name: Conclude attainment
nodes.statement: As $\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n$ was arbitrary, this proves $G_1(\lambda^*)\geq f^*$, which combined with $G_1(\lambda^*)\leq f^*$ yields the desired result $G_1(\lambda^*)=f^*$.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude $G_1(\lambda^*)=f^*$.

nodes.name: Contrast with LP-relaxations for convex programs
nodes.statement: Observe that this does not hold for the LP-relaxations (\ref{kriv-cert}) where generically $\theta_d<f^*$ for every $d\in\mathbb{N}$; see e.g. \cite{Lasserre02a,lasserre-imperial}.

nodes.name: Difficulties of the Lagrangian hierarchy
nodes.statement: Problem (\ref{newhierarchy-def1}) is convex but in general the objective function $G_d$ is non differentiable. Moreover, another difficulty is the computation of $G_d(\lambda)$ for each $\lambda\geq0$ since $G_d(\lambda)$ is the global optimum of the possibly non convex function $(\mathbf{x},\lambda)\mapsto L_d(\mathbf{x},\lambda)$ defined in (\ref{functionL}).
nodes.section: 3 A parametrized hierarchy of\\ semidefinite relaxations
nodes.statement_short: $G_d$ is nondifferentiable in general and each evaluation requires a global nonconvex minimization of $L_d$.

nodes.name: LP-relaxations as Lagrangian with L_d - t identically zero
nodes.statement: Observe that the LP-relaxations (\ref{kriv-cert}) can be written \begin{equation} \theta_d\,=\,\max_{\lambda\geq0,t}\:\left\{\:t\::\: L_d(\mathbf{x},\lambda)-t\,=\,0,\quad \forall \mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n\:\right\}, \end{equation} where $L_d$ has been defined in (\ref{functionL}).
conclusions: the LP-relaxations (\ref{kriv-cert}) can be written
nodes.statement_short: The LP relaxation equals the Lagrangian hierarchy with $\lambda$ restricted so that $L_d(\cdot,\lambda)-t\equiv0$.

nodes.name: LP-relaxation in Lagrangian form
nodes.statement: \theta_d\,=\,\max_{\lambda\geq0,t}\:\left\{\:t\::\: L_d(\mathbf{x},\lambda)-t\,=\,0,\quad \forall \mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n\:\right\},
nodes.label: lp-interpret

nodes.name: LP-relaxations as brute force simplification
nodes.statement: And so the LP-relaxations (\ref{kriv-cert}) can be interpreted as simplifying (\ref{newhierarchy-def1}) by restricting the nonnegative orthant $\{\lambda: \lambda\geq0\}$ to its subset of $\lambda$'s that make the polynomial $\mathbf{x}\mapsto L(\mathbf{x},\lambda)-t$ constant and equal to zero, instead of being only nonnegative. This subset being a polyhedron, solving (\ref{lp-interpret}) reduces to solving a linear program.
nodes.statement_short: The LP hierarchy restricts the nonnegative orthant of multipliers to the polyhedron making $L_d-t$ the zero polynomial.

nodes.name: Krivine-Stengle certificate as rationale of LP convergence
nodes.statement: At first glance, such an a priori simple and naive brute force simplification might seem unreasonable (to say the least). But of course the LP-relaxations (\ref{kriv-cert}) where not defined this way. Initially, the Sherali-Adams' RLT hierarchy \cite{SheraliAdams90} was introduced for 0/1 programs and finite convergence was proved by using {\it ad hoc} arguments. But in fact, the rationale behind convergence of the more general LP-relaxations (\ref{kriv-cert}) is the Krivine-Stengle positivity certificate \cite[Theorem 2.23]{lasserre-imperial}.

nodes.name: Parametrized hierarchy of semidefinite relaxations q^k_d
nodes.statement: Indeed, one may now impose on the same nonnegative polynomial $\mathbf{x}\mapsto L(\mathbf{x},\lambda)-t$ to be a sum of squares (SOS) polynomial $\sigma$ of degree at most $2k$ (instead of being constant and equal to zero as in (\ref{lp-interpret})), and solve the resulting hierarchy of optimization problems: \begin{equation} \begin{array}{rl} q^k_d\,=\,\displaystyle\max_{\lambda,t,\sigma}&t\\ \mbox{s.t.}&L_d(\mathbf{x},\lambda)-t=\sigma,\quad \forall \mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n\\ &\lambda\geq0,\quad\sigma\in\Sigma[\mathbf{x}]_k\end{array}, \end{equation} with $d=1,2,\ldots$, and parametrized by $k$, fixed.
nodes.section: 3.2 A parametrized hierarchy of semidefinite relaxations
nodes.statement_short: Require $L_d(\cdot,\lambda)-t$ to be an SOS of degree $\leq2k$ instead of zero; maximize $t$, giving $q^k_d$.

nodes.name: Parametrized hierarchy q^k_d
nodes.statement: \begin{array}{rl} q^k_d\,=\,\displaystyle\max_{\lambda,t,\sigma}&t\\ \mbox{s.t.}&L_d(\mathbf{x},\lambda)-t=\sigma,\quad \forall \mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n\\ &\lambda\geq0,\quad\sigma\in\Sigma[\mathbf{x}]_k\end{array},
nodes.section: 3.2 A parametrized hierarchy of semidefinite relaxations
nodes.label: lp-semi-k

nodes.name: q^k_d is a semidefinite program with fixed-size LMI
nodes.statement: To see that (\ref{lp-semi-k}) is a semidefinite program, write \[\mathbf{x}\mapsto L_d(\mathbf{x},\lambda)-t\,:=\,\sum_{\beta\in\mathbb{N}^n_s}L_\beta(\lambda,t)\,\mathbf{x}^\beta,\] where $s=d\max_j[{\rm deg}\,g_j]$ and $L_\beta(\lambda,t)$ is linear in $(\lambda,t)$ for each $\beta\in\mathbb{N}^n_s$. Next, for $k\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $2k\leq s$, let $\mathbf{v}_k(\mathbf{x})$ be the vector of the monomial basis $(\mathbf{x}^\beta)$, $\beta\in\mathbb{N}^n_k$, of $\mathbb{R}[\mathbf{x}]_k$, and write \[\mathbf{v}_k(\mathbf{x})\,\mathbf{v}_k(\mathbf{x})^T\,=\,\sum_{\beta\in\mathbb{N}^n_{2k}}\mathbf{x}^\beta\,\mathbf{B}_\beta,\] for some appropriate real symmetric matrices $(\mathbf{B}_\beta)$, $\beta\in\mathbb{N}^n_{2k}$. Then problem (\ref{lp-semi-k}) is the semidefinite program: \begin{equation} \begin{array}{rcll} q^k_d\,=\,\displaystyle\max_{\lambda,t,\mathbf{Q}}&t&&\\ \mbox{s.t.}&L_\beta(\lambda,t)&=&\langle \mathbf{B}_\beta,\mathbf{Q}\rangle,\quad \forall \beta\in\mathbb{N}^n_{2k}\\ &L_\beta(\lambda,t)&=&0,\quad\forall \beta\in\mathbb{N}^n_s,\:\vert\beta\vert>2k\\ &\lambda&\geq&0;\:\mathbf{Q}=\mathbf{Q}^T\succeq0, \end{array}\end{equation} where $\mathbf{Q}$ is a ${n+k\choose n}\times {n+k\choose n}$ real symmetric matrix.
nodes.section: 3.2 A parametrized hierarchy of semidefinite relaxations
conclusions: problem (\ref{lp-semi-k}) is the semidefinite program
nodes.statement_short: Matching coefficients via Gram matrices turns (3.2) into an SDP with a $\binom{n+k}{n}$-sized PSD matrix $\mathbf{Q}$.

nodes.name: SDP form of q^k_d
nodes.statement: \begin{array}{rcll} q^k_d\,=\,\displaystyle\max_{\lambda,t,\mathbf{Q}}&t&&\\ \mbox{s.t.}&L_\beta(\lambda,t)&=&\langle \mathbf{B}_\beta,\mathbf{Q}\rangle,\quad \forall \beta\in\mathbb{N}^n_{2k}\\ &L_\beta(\lambda,t)&=&0,\quad\forall \beta\in\mathbb{N}^n_s,\:\vert\beta\vert>2k\\ &\lambda&\geq&0;\:\mathbf{Q}=\mathbf{Q}^T\succeq0, \end{array}
nodes.section: 3.2 A parametrized hierarchy of semidefinite relaxations
nodes.label: sdp-k

nodes.name: q^k_d dominates the LP bound
nodes.statement: Of course $q^k_d\geq\theta_d\:(=q^0_d)$ for all $d$ because with $\sigma=0$ one retrieves (\ref{kriv-cert}).
nodes.section: 3.2 A parametrized hierarchy of semidefinite relaxations
conclusions: $q^k_d\geq\theta_d\:(=q^0_d)$ for all $d$

nodes.name: Fixed size of the LMI constraint
nodes.statement: Moreover in the semidefinite program (\ref{sdp-k}), the semidefinite constraint $\mathbf{Q}\succeq0$ is concerned with a real symmetric ${n+k\choose n}\times {n+k\choose n}$ matrix, independently of the rank $d$ in the hierarchy. For instance if $k=1$ then $\sigma$ is a quadratic SOS and $\mathbf{Q}$ has size $(n+1)\times (n+1)$. In other words, even if the number of variables $\lambda=(\lambda_{\alpha\beta})$ increases fast with $d$, the LMI constraint $\mathbf{Q}\succeq0$ has fixed size, in contrast with the semidefinite relaxations (\ref{put-cert}) where the size of the LMIs increases with $d$. And it is a well-known fact that crucial for solving semidefinite program is the size of the LMIs involved rather than the number of variables.
nodes.section: 3.2 A parametrized hierarchy of semidefinite relaxations
nodes.statement_short: The PSD constraint has size $\binom{n+k}{n}$ independent of $d$, unlike the standard SDP hierarchy.

nodes.name: 0/1 polynomial program
nodes.statement: Consider 0/1 programs with $f\in\mathbb{R}[\mathbf{x}]$, and feasible set $\mathbf{K}=\{\mathbf{x}:\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}\leq\mathbf{b}\}\cap\{0,1\}^n$, for some real matrix $\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ and some vector $\mathbf{b}\in\mathbb{R}^m$.

nodes.name: Constraint polynomials g_l for 0/1 programs
nodes.statement: Let $g_\ell(\mathbf{x})=(b-\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x})_\ell$, $\ell=1,\ldots,m$, and $g_0(\mathbf{x})=1$.

nodes.name: Sherali-Adams' RLT hierarchy
nodes.statement: Following the definition of the Sherali-Adams' RLT in \cite{SheraliAdams90}, the resulting linear program at step $d$ in the hierarchy reads: \[\theta_d=\displaystyle\max_{\lambda\geq0,t,h}\left \{ t\::\:f(\mathbf{x})-t\,=\,\sum_{i=1}^nh_i(\mathbf{x})\,x_i(1-x_i)\right.\] \[+\sum_{\ell=0}^m\:\displaystyle\sum_{\stackrel{I,J\subset\{1,\ldots,n\}}{ I\cap J=\emptyset; \vert I\cup J\vert \leq d}} \lambda^\ell_{IJ}\:g_\ell(\mathbf{x})\prod_{i\in I}x_i\prod_{j\in J}(1-x_j);\] \begin{equation} \left.h_i\in\mathbb{R}[\mathbf{x}]_{d-1} \quad i=1,\ldots,n\right\},\end{equation} where $\lambda$ is the nonnegative vector $(\lambda^\ell_{IJ})$.
nodes.statement_short: Step-$d$ RLT LP: $f-t$ equals $\sum h_i x_i(1-x_i)$ plus nonnegative combinations of $g_\ell\prod_I x_i\prod_J(1-x_j)$ with $|I\cup J|\leq d$.

nodes.name: Sherali-Adams RLT LP
nodes.statement: \left.h_i\in\mathbb{R}[\mathbf{x}]_{d-1} \quad i=1,\ldots,n\right\},
nodes.label: sherali-def

nodes.name: Sherali-Adams ignores products of constraints
nodes.statement: So all products between the $g_\ell$'s are ignored (see the paragraph before Lemma 1 in \cite[p. 414]{SheraliAdams90}) even though they might help tighten the relaxations.

nodes.name: P-tilde_d for 0/1 programs
nodes.statement: In this context, the problem $\tilde{\mathbf{P}}_d$ equivalent to $\mathbf{P}$ and defined in (\ref{pbtildeP}) by adding redundant constraints formed with products of original ones, reads: \[\begin{array}{rl} \min\{f(\mathbf{x})\::& \mathbf{x}^\alpha \,x_j(1-x_j)\,=\,0,\: j=1,\ldots,n;\:\alpha\in\mathbb{N}^n_{d-1};\\ &g_\ell(\mathbf{x})\displaystyle\prod_{i\in I}x_j\displaystyle\prod_{j\in J}(1-x_j)\geq0,\quad \ell=0,\ldots,m,\\ &I,J\subset\{1,\ldots,n\};\:I\cap J=\emptyset;\:\vert I\cup J\vert\leq d\}. \end{array}\]
nodes.statement_short: For 0/1 programs, $\tilde{\mathbf{P}}_d$ adds the constraints $\mathbf{x}^\alpha x_j(1-x_j)=0$ and $g_\ell\prod_I x_i\prod_J(1-x_j)\geq0$.

nodes.name: 0/1 analogue of the parametrized SDP hierarchy
nodes.statement: Hence the 0/1 analogue of (\ref{lp-semi-k}) reads \[q^k_d=\displaystyle\max_{\lambda\geq0,t,h}\left \{ t\::\:f(\mathbf{x})-t\,=\,\sigma(\mathbf{x})+\sum_{i=1}^nh_i(\mathbf{x})\,x_i(1-x_i)\right.\] \[+\sum_{\ell=0}^m\:\displaystyle\sum_{\stackrel{I,J\subset\{1,\ldots,n\}}{ I\cap J=\emptyset; \vert I\cup J\vert \leq d}} \lambda^\ell_{IJ}\:g_\ell(\mathbf{x})\prod_{i\in I}x_i\prod_{j\in J}(1-x_j);\] \begin{equation} \left.\sigma\in\Sigma[\mathbf{x}]_{k};\quad h_i\in\mathbb{R}[\mathbf{x}]_{d-1} \quad i=1,\ldots,n\right\}.\end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Sherali-Adams RLT LP augmented with an SOS term $\sigma\in\Sigma[\mathbf{x}]_k$.

nodes.name: 0/1 parametrized SDP hierarchy
nodes.statement: \left.\sigma\in\Sigma[\mathbf{x}]_{k};\quad h_i\in\mathbb{R}[\mathbf{x}]_{d-1} \quad i=1,\ldots,n\right\}.
nodes.label: lp-semi-k-01

nodes.name: First 0/1 relaxation at least as strong as SDP relaxation
nodes.statement: For 0/1 programs with linear or quadratic objective function, and for every $k\geq1$, the first semidefinite relaxation (\ref{lp-semi-k-01}), i.e., with $d=2$, is at least as powerful as that of the standard hierarchy of semidefinite relaxations (\ref{put-cert}).
assumptions: 0/1 programs with linear or quadratic objective function
conclusions: the first semidefinite relaxation (\ref{lp-semi-k-01}), i.e., with $d=2$, is at least as powerful as that of the standard hierarchy of semidefinite relaxations (\ref{put-cert})

nodes.name: Justification of Claim (first 0/1 relaxation)
nodes.statement: Indeed (\ref{lp-semi-k-01}) contains products $g_\ell(\mathbf{x})x_j$ or $g_\ell(\mathbf{x})(1-x_k)$, for all $(\ell,j,k)$, which do to not appear in (\ref{put-cert}) with $d=1$.
nodes.statement_short: Direct: (3.5) contains products $g_\ell x_j$, $g_\ell(1-x_k)$ absent from the first SDP relaxation.

nodes.name: Goemans-Williamson guarantee for MAXCUT
nodes.statement: And so in particular, the first such relaxation for MAXCUT has the celebrated Goemans-Williamson's performance guarantee while the standard LP-relaxations (\ref{kriv-cert}) do not.
conclusions: the first such relaxation for MAXCUT has the celebrated Goemans-Williamson's performance guarantee
the standard LP-relaxations (\ref{kriv-cert}) do not

nodes.name: Sherali-Adams + SDP integrality gaps (Benabbas-Magen)
nodes.statement: On the other hand, for 0/1 problems and for the parameter value $k=1$, the hierarchy (\ref{lp-semi-k-01}) is what is called the {\it Sherali-Adams + SDP} hierarchy (basic SDP-relaxation + RLT hierarchy) in e.g. Benabas and Magen \cite{benabbas1} and Benabbas et al. \cite{benabbas2}; and in \cite{benabbas1,benabbas2} the authors show that any (constant) level $d$ of this hierarchy, viewed as a strengthening of the basic SDP-relaxation, does not make the integrality gap decrease.
nodes.origin_citation: Benabbas & Magen 2010; Benabbas, Georgiou, Magen, Tulsiani 2012
conclusions: any (constant) level $d$ of this hierarchy, viewed as a strengthening of the basic SDP-relaxation, does not make the integrality gap decrease
nodes.statement_short: For $k=1$ the 0/1 hierarchy is the Sherali-Adams + SDP hierarchy, whose constant levels do not reduce the integrality gap of the basic SDP.

nodes.name: Sherali-Adams + SDP as level-1 strengthening of RLT
nodes.statement: In fact, and in view of our previous analysis, the ``Sherali-Adams + SDP" hierarchy should be viewed as a {\it (level $k=1$)}-strengthening of the basic Sherali-Adams' LP-hierarchy (\ref{sherali-def}) rather than a strengthening of the basic SDP relaxation.

nodes.name: First-step exactness of the parametrized hierarchy for convex problems
nodes.statement: With $\mathbf{P}$ as in (\ref{def-pb})-(\ref{setk}) let $f,-g_j$ be convex, $j=1,\ldots,m$, let Slater's condition hold and let $f^*>-\infty$. Then: (a) If $\max[{\rm deg}\,f,\:{\rm deg}\,g_j]\leq 2$ then $q^1_1=f^*$, i.e., the first relaxation of the hierarchy (\ref{lp-semi-k}) parametrized by $k=1$, is exact. (a) If $\max[{\rm deg}\,f,\:{\rm deg}\,g_j]\leq 2k$ and $f,-g_j$ are all SOS-convex, then $q^k_1=f^*$, i.e., the first relaxation of the hierarchy (\ref{lp-semi-k}) parametrized by $k$, is exact.
assumptions: let Slater's condition hold and let $f^*>-\infty$
$\max[{\rm deg}\,f,\:{\rm deg}\,g_j]\leq 2k$ and $f,-g_j$ are all SOS-convex
conclusions: $q^1_1=f^*$, i.e., the first relaxation of the hierarchy (\ref{lp-semi-k}) parametrized by $k=1$, is exact
$q^k_1=f^*$, i.e., the first relaxation of the hierarchy (\ref{lp-semi-k}) parametrized by $k$, is exact
nodes.statement_short: For convex problems with Slater's condition, $q^1_1=f^*$ for quadratic data and $q^k_1=f^*$ for SOS-convex data of degree $\leq2k$.
nodes.label: th-final

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.1
nodes.statement: Under the assumptions of Theorem \ref{th-final}, $\mathbf{P}$ has a minimizer $\mathbf{x}^*\in\mathbf{K}$ and the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker optimality conditions hold at $(\mathbf{x}^*,\lambda^*)\in\mathbf{K}\times\mathbb{R}^m_+$ for some $\lambda^*\in\mathbb{R}^m_+$. And so if $k=1$, the Lagrangian polynomial $L_1(\cdot,\lambda^*)-f^*$ is a nonnegative quadratic polynomial and so an SOS $\sigma^*\in\Sigma[\mathbf{x}]_1$. Therefore as $q^1_d\leq f^*$ for all $d$, the triplet $(\lambda^*,f^*,\sigma^*)$ is an optimal solution of (\ref{lp-semi-k}) with $k=d=1$, which proves (a). Next, if $k>1$ and $f,-g_j$ are all SOS-convex then so is the Lagrangian polynomial $L_1(\cdot,\lambda^*)-f^*$. In addition, as $\nabla_\mathbf{x} L_1(\mathbf{x}^*,\lambda^*)=0$ and $L_1(\mathbf{x}^*,\lambda^*)-f^*=0$, the polynomial $L_1(\cdot,\lambda^*)-f^*$ is SOS; see e.g. Helton and Nie \cite[Lemma 4.2]{nie-helton-survey}. Hence $L_1(\cdot,\lambda^*)-f^*=\sigma^*$ for some $\sigma^*\in\Sigma[\mathbf{x}]_k$, and again, the triplet $(\lambda^*,f^*,\sigma^*)$ is an optimal solution of (\ref{lp-semi-k}) with $d=1$, which proves (b).
nodes.statement_short: KKT multipliers make $L_1(\cdot,\lambda^*)-f^*$ a nonnegative quadratic (hence SOS) or an SOS-convex polynomial vanishing with its gradient at $\mathbf{x}^*$ (hence SOS), giving a feasible optimal triplet.

nodes.name: KKT conditions
nodes.statement: Under the assumptions of Theorem \ref{th-final}, $\mathbf{P}$ has a minimizer $\mathbf{x}^*\in\mathbf{K}$ and the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker optimality conditions hold at $(\mathbf{x}^*,\lambda^*)\in\mathbf{K}\times\mathbb{R}^m_+$ for some $\lambda^*\in\mathbb{R}^m_+$.
nodes.statement_short: Existence of a minimizer and KKT multipliers $\lambda^*$.

nodes.name: Case k=1
nodes.statement: And so if $k=1$, the Lagrangian polynomial $L_1(\cdot,\lambda^*)-f^*$ is a nonnegative quadratic polynomial and so an SOS $\sigma^*\in\Sigma[\mathbf{x}]_1$. Therefore as $q^1_d\leq f^*$ for all $d$, the triplet $(\lambda^*,f^*,\sigma^*)$ is an optimal solution of (\ref{lp-semi-k}) with $k=d=1$, which proves (a).
nodes.statement_short: For $k=1$ the Lagrangian minus $f^*$ is a nonnegative quadratic, hence SOS; part (a).

nodes.name: Case k>1 (SOS-convex)
nodes.statement: Next, if $k>1$ and $f,-g_j$ are all SOS-convex then so is the Lagrangian polynomial $L_1(\cdot,\lambda^*)-f^*$. In addition, as $\nabla_\mathbf{x} L_1(\mathbf{x}^*,\lambda^*)=0$ and $L_1(\mathbf{x}^*,\lambda^*)-f^*=0$, the polynomial $L_1(\cdot,\lambda^*)-f^*$ is SOS; see e.g. Helton and Nie \cite[Lemma 4.2]{nie-helton-survey}. Hence $L_1(\cdot,\lambda^*)-f^*=\sigma^*$ for some $\sigma^*\in\Sigma[\mathbf{x}]_k$, and again, the triplet $(\lambda^*,f^*,\sigma^*)$ is an optimal solution of (\ref{lp-semi-k}) with $d=1$, which proves (b).
nodes.statement_short: SOS-convex Lagrangian vanishing with its gradient at $\mathbf{x}^*$ is SOS (Helton-Nie); part (b).

nodes.name: Price of the parametrized hierarchy
nodes.statement: Hence by simplifying (\ref{newhierarchy-def}) in a less brutal manner than in (\ref{kriv-cert}) one recovers a nice and highly desirable property for the resulting hierarchy. The price to pay is to pass from solving a hierarchy of LPs to solving hierarchy of semidefinite programs; however the increase in complexity is controlled by the parameter $k$ since the size of the LMI in the semidefinite program (\ref{sdp-k}) is $O(n^k)$, independently of the rank $d$ in the hierarchy.

nodes.name: Obstruction to exactness of the parametrized hierarchy
nodes.statement: Let $\mathbf{P}$ be as in (\ref{def-pb})-(\ref{setk}) and let Assumption \ref{ass1} hold. Let $\mathbf{x}^*\in\mathbf{K}$ be a global minimizer and let $I_1(\mathbf{x}^*):=\{j\in\{1,\ldots,m\}:\,g_j(\mathbf{x}^*)=0\}$ and $I_2(\mathbf{x}^*):=\{j\in\{1,\ldots,m\}:\,(1-g_j(\mathbf{x}^*))=0\}$ be the set of active constraints at $\mathbf{x}^*$. Let $0\leq k\in\mathbb{N}$ be fixed. The level-$d$ semidefinite relaxation (\ref{lp-semi-k}) is exact only if $f^*$ (resp. $\mathbf{x}^*\in\mathbf{K}$) is also the global optimum (resp. a global minimizer) for the problem \begin{equation} \min_\mathbf{x}\:\{f(\mathbf{x})\::\: \mathbf{x}\in \mathbf{V}\},\end{equation} where $\mathbf{V}\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ (see (\ref{real-variety}) below) is a variety defined from some products of the polynomials $g_j$'s and $(1-g_j)$'s. And if $k=0$ then $f$ must be constant on the variety $\mathbf{V}$.
assumptions: $\mathbf{P}$ be as in (\ref{def-pb})-(\ref{setk}) and let Assumption \ref{ass1} hold
conclusions: The level-$d$ semidefinite relaxation (\ref{lp-semi-k}) is exact only if $f^*$ (resp. $\mathbf{x}^*\in\mathbf{K}$) is also the global optimum (resp. a global minimizer) for the problem
if $k=0$ then $f$ must be constant on the variety $\mathbf{V}$
nodes.statement_short: Exactness of level $d$ forces $\mathbf{x}^*$ to minimize $f$ on a variety $\mathbf{V}$ cut out by products of active constraints; for $k=0$, $f$ is constant on $\mathbf{V}$.

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 4.1
nodes.statement: If (\ref{lp-semi-k}) is exact at level $d\in\mathbb{N}$, then \[L_d(\mathbf{x},\lambda^*)-f^*=\sigma(\mathbf{x}),\qquad\forall \mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n,\] for some $\lambda^*\geq0$ and some $\sigma\in\Sigma[\mathbf{x}]_k$. Equivalently, \begin{eqnarray*} f(\mathbf{x})-f^*\,=\,\sigma(\mathbf{x})&+&\sum_{(\alpha,\beta)\in\mathbb{N}^{2m}_{d}}\lambda^*_{\alpha\beta}\left(\prod_{j=1}^mg_j(\mathbf{x})^{\alpha_j}\right)\times\\ &&\left(\prod_{j=1}^m(1-g_j(\mathbf{x}))^{\beta_j}\right).\end{eqnarray*} Then evaluating at $\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{x}^*$ yields $\sigma(\mathbf{x}^*)=0$ and \[\lambda^*_{\alpha\beta}\,>0\,\Rightarrow\quad\left\{\begin{array}{l} \exists j\in I_1(\mathbf{x}^*)\mbox{ s.t. }\alpha_j>0,\:\mbox{or}\\ \exists j\in I_2(\mathbf{x}^*)\mbox{ s.t. }\beta_j>0.\end{array}\right.\] So let $\Omega\,:=\,\{(\alpha,\beta)\in\mathbb{N}^{2m}_{d}\::\:\lambda^*_{\alpha\beta}>0\}$ and for every $(\alpha,\beta)\in\Omega$ let \begin{eqnarray*} J^1_{\alpha\beta}&:=&\,\{j\in I_1(\mathbf{x}^*)\,:\,\alpha_j>0\},\\ J^2_{\alpha\beta}&:=&\{j\in I_2(\mathbf{x}^*)\,:\,\beta_j>0\}.\end{eqnarray*} Next, define $\mathbf{V}\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ to be the real variety: \begin{eqnarray} \nonumber \left\{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n\right.&:& \left(\prod_{j\in J^1_{\alpha\beta}}g_j(\mathbf{x})\right) \left(\prod_{j\in J^2_{\alpha\beta}}(1-g_j(\mathbf{x}))\right)\,=\,0,\\ &&\left.\forall\:(\alpha,\beta)\in\Omega\:\right\}.\end{eqnarray} Then for every $\mathbf{x}\in\mathbf{V}$, one obtains $f(\mathbf{x})-f^*=\sigma(\mathbf{x})\geq0$, which means that $f^*$ is the global minimum of $f$ on $\mathbf{V}$. If $k=0$ then $\sigma$ is constant and equal to zero. And so $f(\mathbf{x})-f^*=0$ for all $\mathbf{x}\in\mathbf{V}$.
nodes.statement_short: Write the exact certificate, evaluate at $\mathbf{x}^*$ to see which multipliers can be positive, and restrict to the variety where those products vanish.

nodes.name: Exact certificate
nodes.statement: If (\ref{lp-semi-k}) is exact at level $d\in\mathbb{N}$, then \[L_d(\mathbf{x},\lambda^*)-f^*=\sigma(\mathbf{x}),\qquad\forall \mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n,\] for some $\lambda^*\geq0$ and some $\sigma\in\Sigma[\mathbf{x}]_k$. Equivalently, \begin{eqnarray*} f(\mathbf{x})-f^*\,=\,\sigma(\mathbf{x})&+&\sum_{(\alpha,\beta)\in\mathbb{N}^{2m}_{d}}\lambda^*_{\alpha\beta}\left(\prod_{j=1}^mg_j(\mathbf{x})^{\alpha_j}\right)\times\\ &&\left(\prod_{j=1}^m(1-g_j(\mathbf{x}))^{\beta_j}\right).\end{eqnarray*}
nodes.statement_short: Exactness yields an SOS-plus-products certificate for $f-f^*$.

nodes.name: Evaluate at the minimizer
nodes.statement: Then evaluating at $\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{x}^*$ yields $\sigma(\mathbf{x}^*)=0$ and \[\lambda^*_{\alpha\beta}\,>0\,\Rightarrow\quad\left\{\begin{array}{l} \exists j\in I_1(\mathbf{x}^*)\mbox{ s.t. }\alpha_j>0,\:\mbox{or}\\ \exists j\in I_2(\mathbf{x}^*)\mbox{ s.t. }\beta_j>0.\end{array}\right.\]
nodes.statement_short: Evaluating at $\mathbf{x}^*$: $\sigma(\mathbf{x}^*)=0$ and positive multipliers involve active constraints.

nodes.name: Define Omega, J and variety V
nodes.statement: So let $\Omega\,:=\,\{(\alpha,\beta)\in\mathbb{N}^{2m}_{d}\::\:\lambda^*_{\alpha\beta}>0\}$ and for every $(\alpha,\beta)\in\Omega$ let \begin{eqnarray*} J^1_{\alpha\beta}&:=&\,\{j\in I_1(\mathbf{x}^*)\,:\,\alpha_j>0\},\\ J^2_{\alpha\beta}&:=&\{j\in I_2(\mathbf{x}^*)\,:\,\beta_j>0\}.\end{eqnarray*} Next, define $\mathbf{V}\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ to be the real variety: \begin{eqnarray} \nonumber \left\{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n\right.&:& \left(\prod_{j\in J^1_{\alpha\beta}}g_j(\mathbf{x})\right) \left(\prod_{j\in J^2_{\alpha\beta}}(1-g_j(\mathbf{x}))\right)\,=\,0,\\ &&\left.\forall\:(\alpha,\beta)\in\Omega\:\right\}.\end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Define index sets and the real variety $\mathbf{V}$.

nodes.name: f* is the minimum on V
nodes.statement: Then for every $\mathbf{x}\in\mathbf{V}$, one obtains $f(\mathbf{x})-f^*=\sigma(\mathbf{x})\geq0$, which means that $f^*$ is the global minimum of $f$ on $\mathbf{V}$.
nodes.statement_short: On $\mathbf{V}$, $f-f^*=\sigma\geq0$.

nodes.name: Case k=0
nodes.statement: If $k=0$ then $\sigma$ is constant and equal to zero. And so $f(\mathbf{x})-f^*=0$ for all $\mathbf{x}\in\mathbf{V}$.
nodes.statement_short: For $k=0$, $\sigma=0$ so $f$ is constant on $\mathbf{V}$.

nodes.name: Restrictiveness of exactness
nodes.statement: Hence Corollary \ref{badnews} shows that exactness at some step $d$ of the hierarchy (\ref{lp-semi-k}) imposes rather restrictive conditions on problem $\mathbf{P}$. Namely, the global optimum $f^*$ (resp. the global minimizer $\mathbf{x}^*\in\mathbf{K}$) must also be the global optimum (resp. a global minimizer) of problem (\ref{pb-variety}). For instance, suppose that only one constraint, say $g_k(\mathbf{x})\geq0$, is active at $\mathbf{x}^*$. Then $f^*$ (resp. $\mathbf{x}^*$) is also the global minimum (resp. a global minimizer) of $f$ on the variety $\{\mathbf{x}\,:\,g_k(\mathbf{x})=0\}$. And if $k=0$ then $f$ must be constant on the variety $\mathbf{V}$!
nodes.statement_short: Exactness forces $f^*$ to be the minimum of $f$ on a variety; e.g. with one active constraint, on its zero set.

nodes.name: Polytope with one active constraint
nodes.statement: If $\mathbf{K}$ is the (compact) polytope $\{\mathbf{x}: \mathbf{a}_j^T \mathbf{x}\leq 1,\,j=1,\ldots,m\}$ for some vectors $(\mathbf{a}_j)\subset\mathbb{R}^n$, then invoking a result by Handelman \cite{Handelman88}, one does not need the polynomials $\{1-g_j\}$ in the definition (\ref{functionL}) of $L_d$. So for instance, suppose that $I_1(\mathbf{x}^*)=\{\ell\}$ at a global minimizer $\mathbf{x}^*\in\mathbf{K}$. Then exactness at some step $d$ of the hierarchy (\ref{lp-semi-k}) imposes that $f^*$ should also be the global minimum of $f$ on the whole hyperplane $\mathbf{V}=\{\mathbf{x}: \mathbf{a}_\ell^T\mathbf{x}=1\}$; for non convex functions $f$, this is a serious restriction. Moreover, if $k=0$ then $f$ must be constant on the hyperplane $\mathbf{V}$.

nodes.name: Obstruction to exactness of Sherali-Adams RLT
nodes.statement: Let $\mathbf{K}=\{\mathbf{x}:\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}\leq\mathbf{b}\}\cap\{0,1\}^n$ and let $\mathbf{x}^*\in\mathbf{K}$ be an optimal solution of $f^*=\min \{f(\mathbf{x}):\mathbf{x}\in\mathbf{K}\}$. Assume that $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}^*<\mathbf{b}$, i.e., no constraint is active at $\mathbf{x}^*$. (a) The Sherali-Adams' RLT relaxation (\ref{sherali-def}) is exact at step $d$ in the hierarchy only if $f(\mathbf{x})=f(\mathbf{x}^*)=f^*$ for all $\mathbf{x}$ in the set \[\mathbf{V}:=\{\mathbf{x}\in\{0,1\}^n\::\:\prod_{i\in I}x_i\prod_{j\in J}(1-x_j)=0,\quad (I,J)\in Q\},\] where $Q$ is some finite set of couples $(I,J)$ satisfying $I\cap J=\emptyset$ and $\vert I\cup J\vert\leq d$. (b) Similarly, the semidefinite relaxation (\ref{lp-semi-k-01}) is exact at step $d$ only if $\mathbf{x}^*$ is also a global minimizer of $\min \{f(\mathbf{x})\,:\:\mathbf{x}\in\mathbf{V}\}$ for some $\mathbf{V}$ as in (a).
assumptions: $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}^*<\mathbf{b}$, i.e., no constraint is active at $\mathbf{x}^*$
conclusions: The Sherali-Adams' RLT relaxation (\ref{sherali-def}) is exact at step $d$ in the hierarchy only if $f(\mathbf{x})=f(\mathbf{x}^*)=f^*$ for all $\mathbf{x}$ in the set

the semidefinite relaxation (\ref{lp-semi-k-01}) is exact at step $d$ only if $\mathbf{x}^*$ is also a global minimizer of $\min \{f(\mathbf{x})\,:\:\mathbf{x}\in\mathbf{V}\}$ for some $\mathbf{V}$ as in (a)
nodes.statement_short: With no active constraint at $\mathbf{x}^*$, exactness of RLT forces $f$ constant on a subset $\mathbf{V}$ of the cube, and exactness of the SDP variant forces $\mathbf{x}^*$ to minimize $f$ on $\mathbf{V}$.
nodes.label: sherali-exact

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 4.2
nodes.statement: (a) Exactness implies that the polynomial $\mathbf{x}\mapsto f(\mathbf{x})-f^*$ has the representation described in (\ref{sherali-def}) for some polynomials $(h_i)\subset\mathbb{R}[\mathbf{x}]_{d-2}$ and some nonnegative scalars $(\lambda^\ell_{IJ})$. Evaluating both sides of (\ref{sherali-def}) at $\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{x}^*$ and using $g_\ell(\mathbf{x}^*)>0$ for all $\ell=0,\ldots,m$, yields \begin{equation} \lambda_{IJ}^\ell>0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\prod_{i\in I}x^*_i\prod_{j\in J}(1-x^*_j)=0.\end{equation} Let $\mathbf{V}$ be as in Corollary \ref{sherali-exact} with $Q:=\{(I,J)\::\:\mbox{$\exists\,\ell$ s.t. }\lambda^\ell_{IJ}>0\}$. Then from the representation of $\mathbf{x}\mapsto f(\mathbf{x})-f^*$ in (\ref{sherali-def}) we obtain $\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x})-f^*=0$ for all $\mathbf{x}\in\mathbf{V}$ and the result follows. For (b) a similar argument is valid but now using the representation of $f(\mathbf{x})-f^*$ described in (\ref{lp-semi-k-01}). And so exactness yields (\ref{aux-sherali}) as well as $\sigma(\mathbf{x}^*)=0$. Next, for every $\mathbf{x}\in \mathbf{V}$ we now obtain $f(\mathbf{x})-f^*=\sigma(\mathbf{x})\geq0$ because $\sigma$ is SOS.
nodes.statement_short: Evaluate the exact RLT (resp. SOS-augmented) certificate at $\mathbf{x}^*$ to identify vanishing products, then restrict the certificate to the set $\mathbf{V}$ they define.

nodes.name: Part (a)
nodes.statement: (a) Exactness implies that the polynomial $\mathbf{x}\mapsto f(\mathbf{x})-f^*$ has the representation described in (\ref{sherali-def}) for some polynomials $(h_i)\subset\mathbb{R}[\mathbf{x}]_{d-2}$ and some nonnegative scalars $(\lambda^\ell_{IJ})$. Evaluating both sides of (\ref{sherali-def}) at $\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{x}^*$ and using $g_\ell(\mathbf{x}^*)>0$ for all $\ell=0,\ldots,m$, yields \begin{equation} \lambda_{IJ}^\ell>0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\prod_{i\in I}x^*_i\prod_{j\in J}(1-x^*_j)=0.\end{equation} Let $\mathbf{V}$ be as in Corollary \ref{sherali-exact} with $Q:=\{(I,J)\::\:\mbox{$\exists\,\ell$ s.t. }\lambda^\ell_{IJ}>0\}$. Then from the representation of $\mathbf{x}\mapsto f(\mathbf{x})-f^*$ in (\ref{sherali-def}) we obtain $\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x})-f^*=0$ for all $\mathbf{x}\in\mathbf{V}$ and the result follows.
nodes.statement_short: Part (a): exact RLT certificate restricted to $\mathbf{V}$.

nodes.name: Exact RLT certificate
nodes.statement: (a) Exactness implies that the polynomial $\mathbf{x}\mapsto f(\mathbf{x})-f^*$ has the representation described in (\ref{sherali-def}) for some polynomials $(h_i)\subset\mathbb{R}[\mathbf{x}]_{d-2}$ and some nonnegative scalars $(\lambda^\ell_{IJ})$.
nodes.statement_short: Exactness gives an RLT representation of $f-f^*$.

nodes.name: Evaluate at x*
nodes.statement: Evaluating both sides of (\ref{sherali-def}) at $\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{x}^*$ and using $g_\ell(\mathbf{x}^*)>0$ for all $\ell=0,\ldots,m$, yields \begin{equation} \lambda_{IJ}^\ell>0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\prod_{i\in I}x^*_i\prod_{j\in J}(1-x^*_j)=0.\end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Positive multipliers force the corresponding product to vanish at $\mathbf{x}^*$.

nodes.name: Restrict to V
nodes.statement: Let $\mathbf{V}$ be as in Corollary \ref{sherali-exact} with $Q:=\{(I,J)\::\:\mbox{$\exists\,\ell$ s.t. }\lambda^\ell_{IJ}>0\}$. Then from the representation of $\mathbf{x}\mapsto f(\mathbf{x})-f^*$ in (\ref{sherali-def}) we obtain $\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x})-f^*=0$ for all $\mathbf{x}\in\mathbf{V}$ and the result follows.
nodes.statement_short: On $\mathbf{V}$ the certificate gives $f=f^*$.

nodes.name: Part (b)
nodes.statement: For (b) a similar argument is valid but now using the representation of $f(\mathbf{x})-f^*$ described in (\ref{lp-semi-k-01}). And so exactness yields (\ref{aux-sherali}) as well as $\sigma(\mathbf{x}^*)=0$. Next, for every $\mathbf{x}\in \mathbf{V}$ we now obtain $f(\mathbf{x})-f^*=\sigma(\mathbf{x})\geq0$ because $\sigma$ is SOS.
nodes.statement_short: Part (b): same argument with the SOS term, giving $f-f^*=\sigma\geq0$ on $\mathbf{V}$.

nodes.name: Vanishing products at x*
nodes.statement: \lambda_{IJ}^\ell>0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\prod_{i\in I}x^*_i\prod_{j\in J}(1-x^*_j)=0.

nodes.name: Role of constraints in V and singleton case
nodes.statement: The constraints $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}\leq\mathbf{b}$ play no explicit role in the definition of the set $\mathbf{V}$. Moreover, if $f$ discriminates all points of the hypercube $\{0,1\}^n$ then exactness of the Sherali-Adams' RLT implies that $\mathbf{V}$ must be the singleton $\{\mathbf{x}^*\}$.

nodes.name: Extended Lagrangian relaxation
nodes.statement: For each $d\in\mathbb{N}$, problem (\ref{ex-lagrangian}) is an obvious relaxation of $\mathbf{P}$ and in fact is an {\it extended Lagrangian relaxation} of $\mathbf{P}$ where the multipliers are now allowed to be SOS polynomials with a degree bound, instead of constant nonnegative polynomials (i.e., SOS polynomials of degree zero).

differentia: the multipliers are now allowed to be SOS polynomials with a degree bound, instead of constant nonnegative polynomials

nodes.name: Convergence of the extended Lagrangian relaxation
nodes.statement: If $\mathbf{K}$ is compact and the quadratic module \[Q(g)\,:=\,\{\sum_{j=0}^m\sigma_j\,g_j\::\:\sigma_j\in\Sigma[\mathbf{x}],\quad j=0,1,\ldots,m\}\] (where $g_0=1$) is Archimedean, then $\omega_d\to f^*$ as $d\to\infty$.

nodes.name: SDP relaxations simplify the extended Lagrangian relaxation
nodes.statement: In fact, writing (\ref{ex-lagrangian}) as \begin{eqnarray*} \omega_d=\max_{t,\sigma}\{t&:&f(\mathbf{x})-\sum_{j=1}^m\sigma_j(\mathbf{x})\,g_j(\mathbf{x})-t\,\geq\,0\quad\forall\mathbf{x}\,;\\ &&{\rm deg}(\sigma_jg_j)\leq 2d\},\end{eqnarray*} the semidefinite relaxations (\ref{put-cert}) simplify (\ref{ex-lagrangian}) by imposing on the nonnegative polynomial $\mathbf{x}\mapsto f(\mathbf{x})-\sum_j\sigma_j(\mathbf{x})g_j(\mathbf{x})-t$ to be an SOS polynomial $\sigma_0\in\Sigma[\mathbf{x}]_d$ (rather than just being nonnegative).
nodes.section: On the hierarchy of semidefinite relaxations
nodes.statement_short: The standard SDP hierarchy replaces nonnegativity of the extended Lagrangian minus $t$ by an SOS condition.

nodes.name: Different spirit of the SDP hierarchy; no obstruction to exactness
nodes.statement: But the spirit is different from the LP-relaxations as there is no problem $\tilde{\mathbf{P}}_d$ obtained from $\mathbf{P}$ by adding finitely many redundant constraints and equivalent to $\mathbf{P}$. Instead of adding more and more redundant constraints and doing a standard Lagrangian relaxation to $\tilde{\mathbf{P}}_d$, one applies an extended Lagrangian relaxation to $\mathbf{P}$ with SOS multipliers of increasing degree (instead of nonnegative scalars). And in contrast to LP-relaxations, there is no obstruction to exactness (i.e., finite convergence). In fact, it is quite the opposite since as demonstrated recently in Nie \cite{nie2012}, finite convergence is generic!
